Title: Marco Rubio to Outline His Approach to Foreign Policy

Marco Rubio and the Obama Doctrine is a slightly saltier version of “Don’t Do Stupid Stuff.” The Bush Doctrine argued for preventive strikes in the interest of self-defense and national security.
"As America, we shall fight for an adequate number of forces within our borders to keep peace with the world. And that means we must ensure that the United States does not interfere in the internal affairs of others and should not violate international law, with or without a court-order. We must not interfere with the ability of other states, states' allies, countries to intervene in our own internal affairs,‡ or in our country’s own domestic politics."
That's the idea behind the George W. Bush doctrine, which was in its core outline when Mr. Rubio was governor of Florida in 2000. The Bush doctrine has been championed by American conservatives who argue that countries can be relied on to protect others from threats like terrorism and international terrorism. And when a country threatens to enter into diplomatic and military conflicts, the United States can act to intervene in that case, as it did during the Cold War, by seizing military bases or conducting military operations.
But that doctrine has not been adopted by the Bush administration. And the concept hasn't been in the official lexicon of foreign policy at all since the U.S. was formally given the title of "partner of the United States" at the end of World War II when the United States invaded Czechoslovakia.
The concept of providing "security assistance," as it is known in international law, has been around since the 1920s.
But it was not until the United States became the undisputed leader in global disarmament that the concept of the United States as a "nonaligned sovereign state" was taken to a whole new level.
The concept of "nonaligned sovereignty," based on the view that any nations that have not accepted U.S. leadership are the main antagonists to that alliance, is the standard on which U.S. policy has consistently been based throughout nearly two decades, according to the National Security Council. But, unlike most treaties and the founding principles of our republic, the United States's foreign policy has never been defined by its allies.
If it was, the United States would have been the only nation to ever accept the "no aggression" rule of an international community. But a country that does not accept the "aggression" rule of an international community would have been considered a threat, under our constitutional system.

This is not to say the religious freedom laws in Indiana and Washington are unconstitutional or even unconstitutional, and they are not the only ones that allow businesses to make this decision.
The Indiana law provides for exemptions from federal law. But those exemptions are only valid for individuals who reside in the states with the law that provides for exemption.
When applying for or renewing a license, the state is allowed to "include a number of items to prove that the applicant has no known affiliation with a business." The exemptions do not apply to religious institutions.
The Indiana law does not apply to public companies, which are subject to the Federal Religious Freedom Restoration Act.
As for those companies that might lose exemption? Their state insurance programs do not cover the cost of implementing the law. But the state has already implemented the law (and the federal law) as of January 2016.
In Indiana, the insurance program for Indiana residents of religious homes is available through the ACA marketplace. This insurance program runs through June 1.
However, it does not cover individual business owners. Indiana law does require that any business that provides services to the general public that "prevents or prohibits discrimination based on age, sex, marital status, political affiliations, religious or other beliefs," or "adversely effects the health, safety, welfare, or safety of the general public, or of any particular individual, by a health, welfare, or safety-related service offered by the consumer under such a provision of the law. Any individual, firm, or corporation that violates these or other laws shall be fined not more than $2,000 or imprisoned not more than 1 year."
Indiana is among the most conservative states in the nation, especially because of its relatively conservative politics. In November, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in a case against the state that, despite its "extreme conservatism," it is still not constitutional.
In other states, like New Mexico and Oregon, citizens of some religious denominations can qualify.

Christie was appointed as governor of New Jersey in a post-9/11 era, after the attacks on September 11, 2001.
In an interview with MSNBC last month, Christie said he was grateful that the attacks had left his state feeling threatened and that he was grateful the federal government didn't intervene. But the federal government's response to 9/11 was never about getting people safe.
In an October 2009 interview with "Fox News Sunday," he recalled his first "bomb bomb" explosion and his personal thoughts on 9/11. "That was an atomic bomb. And I don't know that there's anything more terrifying than an atomic bomb and you have it in your head because we all know what we had."
Christie's personal life was also very personal.
On March 3, 2012, Christie was seen sitting in his home in Livingston, New Jersey after he won the governor's mansion in a landslide election on a promise to reduce federal spending by a quarter after a budget deal struck between the U.S. and Iran in which the nuclear deal would have increased the funding levels for the Department of Energy.
In that election, in which he led the Republican ticket and led the New Jersey Democratic Party, his party's presidential nominee, a Democrat, Christie won 52 percent of the vote. In New Jersey, the Democratic Party received nearly 10 percent of the vote, according to a recent Quinnipiac University Poll.
On October 6, 2011, Christie said he was planning to return to his old job in New Jersey after a long absence. When asked if he had been thinking about leaving New Jersey, he responded with a wink at his former hometown. "I think it's going to go more or less in the right direction. It's about the quality of life and how it plays out. It's about making sure we continue to work our collective way through this crisis in New Jersey," he said.
Since his election to a second term in November 2010, Christie has taken out nearly $20 million in private debt. The state received nearly $100 million in public dollars in 2011.
A September 2012 New York Times article noted that Christie received several large grants from the federal government to help run his reelection bid.
This has fueled speculation about his potential for a run in the 2016 election. While Christie has made few promises about his future, several of his proposals, such as to reform and strengthen social programs, are consistent with his conservative political beliefs.

This week, I was able to meet with several of Chick-fil-A's staff members for our breakfast at home, where they described this business as "the most inclusive environment in the country."
Today, they are not trying to defend this decision. Rather they are trying to call for dialogue.
I have met a number of Chick-fil-A staff members in the past, but not all have been supportive of its position. In April, after an employee came out publicly and told him he opposed same-sex marriage, a local Chick-fil-A customer called my friend and asked why he doesn't want people to be a "convinced person" in the restaurant. I'll come back to that and tell him what he's right to do and what the business is right for.
As we learned last week from the meeting with the customer, in the Chick-fil-A environment there are still many layers of cultural barriers to overcome.
What they do have is a commitment to not allow discrimination. As my colleague John O'Connell commented earlier this month, "Cathy is a strong believer in a pluralistic culture that rejects racialized roles. We're certainly aware of the power of the 'No Sides' principle to push us to think, speak, and feel as equal as possible in order to advance our own culture. But we're still committed to working toward equality at all costs for everyone, especially those of our staff and employees, all over the country."
It is clear to me that Chick-fil-A is the next big movement. But the only way they can change the status quo is by engaging with our own communities and our allies.

Title: Bloomberg says Trump a 'dangerous demagogue,' endorses Clinton at DNC
Summary: Despite strong support from the GOP establishment, a Republican presidential primary challenger won't clinch a majority of the vote in November. Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton has not been a successful candidate as an alternative to Trump. Both of them received strong support from the establishment last year as they worked to win over young voters in swing states and to win control of House seats in 2014. It also appears increasingly likely that Trump has won the GOP nomination, giving the GOP establishment an opportunity to turn the tables on Trump. Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton remains tied to her party's nominee in November and could lose her momentum.
